Isotope definition
The definition of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ are:

$$
\delta ^ { 1 3 } C = \left( \frac { \left( \frac { 1 3 } { 1 2 } C H _ { 4 } \right) _ { s a m p l e } } { \left( \frac { 1 3 } { 1 2 } C \right) _ { V P D B } } - 1 \right) \times 1 , 0 0 0
$$

$$
\delta D = \left( \frac { \left( \frac { C H _ { 3 } D } { C H _ { 4 } } \right) _ { s a m p l e } } { \left( \frac { D } { H } \right) _ { V S M O W } } - 1 \right) \times 1 , 0 0 0
$$

where subscript “sample” denotes the sample, and Vienna Pee Dee belemnite (VPDB) represents the international standard for $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , with $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } / ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { C }$ of $1 , 1 2 3 . 7 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ (Craig, 1957), and the Vienna standard mean ocean water (VSMOW) for $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , with $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { H }$ of $1 5 5 . 7 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 }$ (Hagemann et al., 1970).
The definition of $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } 4$ is following Lassey et al. (2007) as:

$$
\Delta ^ { 1 4 } C = \left( \frac { A _ { S N } } { A _ { a b s } } - 1 \right) \times 1 , 0 0 0
$$

where $A _ { a b s }$ is the “absolute international standard activity” of $0 . 2 2 6 0 \pm 0 . 0 0 1 2 \mathrm { B q g C ^ { - 1 } }$ (Stuiver, 1980), Bq is Becquerel, or disintegrations per second equates to $4 3 3 . 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 5 } \mathrm { m o l e } ( ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C } )$ , and $A _ { S N }$ is the “normalized” sample activity (assumed to be corrected for “shelf” decay between sample collection and $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ analysis) expressed in terms of the measured activity $A _ { S }$ (i.e. $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } ,$ /total $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ of sample) normalized to a $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ of $- 2 5 \text{‰}$ (see Lassey et al. (2007) for more detail).
Observation targets

We set atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , and $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ observational target ranges for 51 target years, 1750, 1850, 1900, 1950, 1960, and every year for 1970–2015 (Fig. S1 and Table S1). The mean and uncertainty of targets, for which the values were not prescribed, were linearly interpolated using the adjacent data. The atmospheric target year is assumed to be at 0:00 UTC, January 1st in each year; thus the annual observational targets are interpolated when adjacent annual mean data is available (e.g., target data at 2000.0 is derived from annal mean in 1999 $( \mathrm { y e a r } = 1 9 9 9 . 5 )$ and in 2000 (year $=$ 2000.5)) (Table S1). Since the setting of atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ is already described in the main text, here we describe how atmospheric $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , and $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } 4$ targets were constructed in more detail.

Since the spatiotemporal coverages of these observations were limited before 1970s, especially for $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , it is difficult to reconstruct annual-basis global observational targets. Thus we adopted multi-decadal blocks of observational target before 1970. To reconstruct the global mean and uncertainty under the sparse data coverage, we often utilized the Arctic and Antarctic data as the boundary value of global tropospheric mean (see below). Although these approaches should weaken their actual observational constraints, we confirmed such historical targets can still constrain the average $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ source and sink parameters, perticularly natural source parameters (see section 3.1 amd Fig. 4 in the main text).

The $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } 4$ target ranges over 1750–1900 and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ over 1750–1970 are assumed to be time-invariant, which are inferred from Antarctic ice-core and firn-air observational data in Ferretti et al. (2005) and Mischler et al. (2009). The target ranges are set to be wide, $[ - 5 0 , - 4 8 ] \textdegree _ { 0 0 }$ for $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $[ - 1 1 5 , - 8 5 ] \ : \%$ for $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , respectively, considering the limited time and space representativeness of the observation, the inter-hemispheric differences in $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \left( \mathrm { - } 0 . 6 \% \right)$ and $ { \delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 } } \left(  { - } 1 6 \% \right)$ (Beck et al., 2018), and their potential inter-laboratory measurement differences (Umezawa et al., 2018). For $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ over 1900-1970, a secular increasing trend, $0 . 0 1 5 \text{‰}$ year, is estimated from the data in Ferretti et al. (2005), Mischler et al. (2009), and Rice et al. (2016). The linear trend is applied to the respective lower and upper bounds of the target from 1900 every 10 years to 1970. It is known that the atmospheric krypton (Kr) can led to biases in $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ during mass spectrometric measurements, estimated to be about $+ 0 . 4 \text{‰}$ on Ferretti et al. (2005) and Mischler et al. (2009)’s $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ data (Schmitt et al., 2013). Also, Ferretti et al. (2005)’s data have not been corrected for diffusive fractionation in the firn air at Law Dome DE-08 site, estimated to be up to $- 0 . 4 \text{‰}$ (the largest during the period of rapid atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ increase around 1970) (Sapart et al., 2013). Since our historical $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ target ranges are specified to be quite wide, allowing a wide range of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ trends over 1750–1970, we assume the potential biases for both $\mathrm { K r }$ interference and diffusive fractionation in Ferretti et al. (2005) and Mischler et al. (2009)’s data are not significant in our analysis.

For 1984–2013, annual mean globally averaged $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ data is taken from SI Figure 3 of Schwietzke et al. (2016), where INSTAAR $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ data is used for 1999–2013 (Michel et al., 2021) and NIWA $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ data is used for 1984–1998 (Schaefer et al., 2016) after unifying to INSTAAR $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ scale (see Schwietzke et al. (2016)). Before 1984, the global average is extrapolated until 1978 using northern hemispheric composite $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ trend in Rice et al. (2016) for 1978–1983 and the mean difference of the global averages from the nortern composite $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ for 1984–2009, $0 . 1 5 \pm$ $0 . 0 4 \text{‰}$ (1 SD). Note that the difference includes both the spatial representative difference and potential inter-laboratory measurement differences (Umezawa et al., 2018).

For $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , the annual mean globally average is derived from global coverage observational network by Tohoku University (TU) for 2006–2013 (Fujita et al., 2020) and INSTAAR for 2006–2009 (except Black Sea, Romania, for the purpose of background site selection) (White et al., 2016) (see Fig. S1). The procedure for obtaining the global averages and uncertainties is as follows (updated from Turner et al. (2017) for obtaining global averages):

1. Compute annual averages of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ at each station using long-term trend to the observed data estimated by a digital-filtering technique (Nakazawa et al., 1997).   
2. Group each annual mean record by 4 latitudinal bands: NET (Northern Extra Tropics: $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N - }$ $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N } )$ ), NTRO (Northern Tropics: $\mathrm { E Q } { - } 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N } )$ , STRO (Southern Tropics: $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S }$ –EQ), and SET (Southern Extra Tropics: $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S } { - } 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S }$ ) and determine the number of sites in each latitude: nNET, nNTRO, nSTRO, and, nSET.   
3. Randomly select $n \chi \chi$ sites from each latitudinal band with replacement.   
4. Compute the zonal means in 4 latitudinal bands from the randomly selected nXX sites and derive global average by averaging the 4 zonal means.   
5. Repeat 1000 times, yielding 1000 different global averages.   
6. Compute the mean global average and standard deviation from the 1000 realizations.

In step 4, a random error of $2 \text{‰}$ (1 SD) is applied when generating the annual mean for each station as the inclusion of measurement uncertainty and spatial representativeness (White et al., 2016; Fujita et al., 2020). The shipboard data in the western Pacific region in Fujita et al. (2020) is combined into 4 latitudinal band $3 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N } { - } 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N }$ , $1 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N - E Q }$ , $2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S } { - } 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S }$ , and $4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S } { - } 2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { S } )$ ), which are grouped into each latitudinal band in step 2 using their mean latitudes. There is no siginificant difference in global averages calculated from either TU or INSTAAR dataset for 2006–2009; thus we combine their data for 2006–2009 and the global averages from TU dataset for 2010–2013. Before 2005, the global average is extrapolated by averaging the NET and SET trends for 1995–2005 (Rice et al., 2016; Fujita et al., 2020) and incorporating the mean difference between global averages and NET and SET averages for 2006–2013 $( 1 . 5 \pm 0 . 2 \% 0 )$ . Additionally, the extrapolation includes the NET trend for 1978– 1994 (Rice et al., 2016) and the mean difference between global averages and NET for 2006–2013 (8.9 $\pm \ : 0 . 4 \text{‰}$ . The potential inter-laboratory differences are added to Rice et al. (2016)’s $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ data $( - 2 . 4$ $\pm \ : 1 . 6 \text{‰}$ (Umezawa et al., 2018) to adjust to the TU $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ scale (Fujita et al., 2020).

The observational $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ targets for 1750–1970 are constructed using the Greenland and Antarctic ice-core and firn-air data in Hmiel et al. (2020). First, the measured data, whose mean age of air is around 25 years from 1750 and 1900 and around 10 years from 1950, 1960, 1970 are selected. Then, the target range in each target year is determined by using the minimum and maximum among these data—mean $\pm 2$ SD of each data in Table S2 of Hmiel et al. (2020). Note that the target range is specified to be wider if the data number is less than three or the dataset does not contain both northern and southern hemispheric data, to take into account the limited spatiotemporal representativeness in the measured data over the period. Only one measurement at Summit, Greenland, is available in 1750, thus the target range is widened by mean $\pm 4$ SD. No northern hemispheric data are available in 1950, thus the measured data at Summit whose mean age of air is 1966 are also used for the target range in 1950. Only one measurement in each hemisphere is available in 1960, thus the target range is widened to mean $\pm 3$ SD. After the 1950s, there is a discernible increasing trend in $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ observed in both hemispheres, which is attributed to biospheric $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions after the 1950s and NPP $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions after the 1970s (Lassey et al., 2007; Hmiel et al., 2020). Following 1980, the availability of $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H _ { 4 } }$ data increases, allowing for the estimation of global averages and uncertainties through spline fitting applied to data from both the northern and southern hemispheres. To account for measurement uncertainties reported in Hmiel et al. (2020), the spline fit is iteratively applied to the data spanning from the 1950s to the 2010s, with uncertainties randomly sampled 5000 times assuming a Gaussian distribution. Subsequently, the global average is determined as the mean of the northern and southern hemispheric data for each year. The uncertainty (1 SD) of the global averages is specified as one quarter of the inter-polar difference of spline fit for each year, assuming that the global averages fall within the two polar values with $9 5 \%$ CI. All the target ranges, constructed as above, encompass independent $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ measurements of firn air in Antarctica for 1940s–1970s and of air sampled globally for 1986–2000 in Lassey et al. (2007), except the data around 1976 $( \sim 1 6 0 \text{‰}$ , which exceeds our original upper bound at 1970 $(11 7 \text{‰}$ . To cover a wider range considering the potential uncertainty of age of air both in Lassey et al. (2007) and Hmiel et al. (2020), we set $160 \text{‰}$ as our upper bound at 1970 (see Table S1).

When we convert global mean surface mole fractions to global atmospheric burden using the conversion factor of $2 . 7 5 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { p p b } ^ { - 1 }$ (Prather et al. 2012), we did not account for the vertical gradient of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , dD- $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , as similar to previous isotope box model studies (e.g., Lassey et al. 2007; Schwietzke et al. 2016; Turner et al. 2017; Hmiel et al. 2020). Therefore, we assumed the same correction factor to account for reduced abundance in the stratosphere for $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { D }$ , and $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ as for total $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ (“fill factor"; see Prather et al. (2012)), although the potential mean differences of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ between the stratosphere $\mathord { \sim } 1 8 \mathrm { k m }$ altitudes in the mid latitudes) and surface are about $+ 1 . 7 \text{‰}$ for $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $+ 2 5 \text{‰}$ for $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $- 5 5 \text{‰}$ for $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , respectively. Here, the stratospheric values for $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ were taken from Röckmann et al. (2011). No $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ data was available in the stratopshere, but since $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ cancels out isotopic fractionations due to loss processes, we can assume only the mean age of air in the stratosphere at 18 $\mathrm { k m }$ (assumed to be 4 year; Waugh and Hall (2002)) would affect the mean difference from the tropospheric $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ . Therefore, the potential maximum difference of $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ between stratosphere and surface over the analysis period is ${ \sim } 5 5 \mathrm { ‰}$ in the latter 1960s when the most rapid changes in $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } 4$ were observed (Fig. S1). Based on the above estimates and the mean air mass ratio between troposphere and stratosphere of 0.8 and 0.2 and corresponding $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ mole fractions of 1800 and $1 5 5 0 \mathrm { p p b }$ (equivalent to fill factor of 0.972; similar to Prather et al. (2012)’s estimate), the impact of potential biases using the same fill factor for $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { D }$ , and $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ are estimated to be 0.3, 5, and $10 \text{‰}$ for the global mean $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ , $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } 4$ , respectively. These are comparable to the uncertainties of our prescribed atmospheric targets and are within the range of potential inter-laboratory differences in these measurements, where we find they do not significantly affect our posterior source fraction estimates (Fig. S12).
Prior emission scenarios

Table S2 shows our three a priori global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ source scenarios using CEDS (version 2017-05- 18) (Hoesly et al., 2018), EDGARv5.0 (Crippa et al., 2020) and EDGARv6.0 (Crippa et al., 2021), together with biomass burning (van Marle et al., 2017), natural biogenic (e.g., wetlands, freshwater) (Saunois et al. 2020) and geologic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources (Etiope & Schwietzke, 2019; Hmiel et al., 2020). Our definition of total anthropogenic fossil emissions include “residential, commercial, and other sectors” (RCO) (Hoesly et al., 2018), whereas Saunois et al. (2020) separated these sectors into biomass burning sources. Thus our prior total anthropogenic fossil emissions are reported to be ${ \sim } 1 0 \mathrm { T g / y r }$ higher than those summarized in Saunois et al. (2020) (and vice versa in biomass burning emissions). We have investigated the sensitivity by moving the RCO emissions from prior anthropogenic FF emissions to prior BB emissions and confirmed that the posterior FF fractions are within the range of our base simulation results (Fig S5).
Comparison among different inventories

The fugitive $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emission estimates in CEDS are based on EDGARv4.2 (Hoesly et al., 2018) and that EDGARv5.0 is based on EDGARv4.3.2 (Crippa et al., 2020), respectively, whose coal $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions in China is reported to be overestimated (e.g., Maasakkers et al. (2019)). The total FF emissions in China in EDGARv6.0 for 2003–2012 is calculated to be $2 4 . 7 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is even $2 . 4 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ higher than those in EDGARv5.0. The difference is mostly explained by upward revision of coal emissions in China in EDGARv6.0, indicating that the overestimated China’s coal emission can still remain in EDGARv6.0. Similar overestimation in China is also seen when applied the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-based emission inventories (Scarpelli et al., 2020) to the atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ inversion (Lu et al., 2021), although the global total anthropogenic emission estimates in UNFCCC are underestimated (IEA, 2022). The EDGARv7.0 is also available (https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg70) (Crippa et al., 2022), but the values are almost the same as EDGARv6.0 until 2018 (Fig. 7). Also newer CEDS version 2021-04-21 is available (O'Rourke et al., 2021), which has higher fossil emissions than the version 2017-05-18 before 2000 but rather lowered after 2003 (Fig. 7). To investigate the robustness of our findings, further studies using other available prior emission inventories (Höglund-Isaksson et al., 2020; O'Rourke et al., 2021; IEA, 2022) are also required.
Spin-up procedure

Our spin-up procedure consists of two steps. First, to initiate the spin-up, the first target year, 1750, was initially compared to the atmospheric values assuming steady state. These atmospheric values were computed by the initial parameter ensembles generated from their full initial ranges using Latin hypercube sampling. The initial ensembles were then resampled based on the likelihood function in 1750. Subsequently, new uniform distributions were created for each parameter, based on the minimum and maximum values from the resampled distributions. These bounds were expanded by $\pm 2 \%$ of the full initial ranges to encompass broader potential parameter solutions. Following this initial approximate optimization, a 50-yr spin-up simulation was further performed with the new parameter ensembles, during which all parameters were prescribed to be constant at their initial values. Finally, new ensembles were once again resampled based on the likelihood function in 1750. As a result of this two step procedure, the posterior ensembles are effectively determined while saving calculation time.
Reported posterior distributions

We report annual posterior $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions and sinks and 20 parameter distributions for $1 7 5 0 -$ 2015 for the CEDS, EDGARv5, and v6 scenarios individually (Fig. 1–6, Fig. S7, and Table S2) or averaged (Fig. 7–12, Table 2, Table 3, Fig. S2–S6, S8–S13, and Table S5). Sensitivity tests
Here, we present the results of our sensitivity tests in Fig. S5–S6, S8–S12, which we did not fully discuss in the main text.

Only a few studies utilized atmospheric $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ data to estimate global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget as additional constraints (Rice et al., 2016; Fujita et al., 2020) and there is no recent studies that solely utilized $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ with atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ , which restricted the detailed investigation on the impact of $\delta \mathbf { D } \cdot$ - $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ . Experimental $\mathrm { K I E ^ { D } o _ { H } }$ ranges 1.29 to 1.31 (Gierczak et al. 1997; Saueressig et al. 2001; Joelsson et al. 2016) except DeMore (1993) as 1.18. Based on the experimental KIED and sink fractions reported in Saunois et al. (2020), sink-weighted total $\mathrm { K I E ^ { D } }$ are calculated to be from 1.275 to 1.300, except when applying DeMore (1993) to $\mathrm { K I E ^ { D } o _ { H } }$ as ${ \sim } 1 . 2 0$ (Table S3). Considering the uncertainty in these estimated range and adopting the total KIED of 1.275 as our prior mean, used in Fujita et al. (2020), as our prior mean, our prior base KIED range was set to be [1.25, 1.30]. Although this range does not fully cover the lower bound of total KIED based on $\mathrm { K I E ^ { D } o _ { H } }$ of DeMore (1993), we attempted to cover the possibility of lower KIED scenario, less than 1.275. Process models suggest stable global wetland emissions for 2000–2012 (Poulter et al., 2017), whereas recent ESMs indicate an increase up to ${ \sim } 3 0 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ since pre-industrial (Paudel et al., 2016; Swart et al., 2019). Emissions from freshwater systems also vary widely $( 1 3 4 { - } 2 8 4 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ in bottom-up and less than $3 0 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ in top-down; Saunois et al. 2020). Our base scenario assumes time-invariant prior wetland and freshwater emissions from GCP bottom-up estimates $( 1 4 7 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ and $1 5 9 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively; Saunois et al. 2020), but with wider uncertainties including timevariable scaling factor $( f _ { n a t r \_ b i o } )$ . To explore the sensitivity of natural BIO (mainly wetlands and freshwater) emissions and trends, four altanative scenarios are also considered: (E) increasing wetland scenario from $1 4 7 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ to $1 8 0 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ for 1850–2015 (Paudel et al., 2016; Swart et al., 2019), (F) using VISIT (Ito, 2021) wetland emissions for 1901–2015 under Walter and Heimann (2000) emission scheme (G) same with (F) but for Cao et al. (1996) emission scheme, and (H) excluding freshwater emissions (IAWetBIOem and NoFRESHem #1). The results show minimal impact on recent $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ trends or mean source fractions for 2003–2012 (Fig S9). However, posterior anthropogenic BIO emissions in scenario E align more closely with CEDS prior emissions than in our base scenario that align with EDGARv5 and v6, despite total BIO emissions being consistent. Therefore, we have presented our posterior BIO emissions mainly for total BIO sources.

We found that “NoFRESHem” scenario (scenario H in Fig. S9) significantly impacts on the posterior source fractions when atmospheric $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ data are not used as constraints, yeilding higher FF fractions compared to those under the base prior emission setting (Fig. S11 and Table S5). (2018)) to our observational target, our posterior FF fractions are derived to be 22.8 [18.9, 26.8] $\%$ and 25.4 [21.8, $2 8 . 7 ] \%$ , respectively. These are within the uncertainty of our base results, $2 3 . 1 \ : [ 1 9 . 0 , 2 6 . 8 ] \ : \%$ , but careful attention should be paid to the impact of $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ offset. No inter-laboratory comparison for $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ measurements has been reported yet, but our sensitivity tests indicate our posterior estimate is robust within $\Delta ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ differences of $\pm 1 5 \text{‰}$ (22.3 [18.0, 26.3] % and $2 4 . 2 [ 2 0 . 0 , 2 8 . 1 ] \%$ of posterior FF fraction, respectively). More careful consideration is required when assimilating historical raw $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ data directly, whose inter-laboratory offsets are much larger than modern air samples (Umezawa et al. 2018). In this regard, we did not utilize respective raw $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta \mathrm { D - C H } _ { 4 }$ data but applied wider multi-decadal target range for historical period, considering their potential large uncertainty to represent global averages.
Sink fractions derived from posterior total ${ \bf K I E ^ { C } }$ and KIED

In the base scenario, we derive higher total $\mathrm { K I E ^ { C } }$ (1.0075 [1.0070, 1.0078]) and KIED (1.283 [1.274, 1.292]) for 2003–2012 than our prior mean setting (Fig. 3), which contributes to balancing the atmospheric $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { D }$ budgets. These parameters are also correlated with BIO and FF fractions in our base ensemble results, but not well correlated among the multiple sensitivity tests, compared with BIO $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ source signatures and NPP factors $( \phi )$ . Here, we assume that the estimated total KIEs are equivalent to the sum of the experimental KIEs of the base setting (refer to Table S4) weighted by the respective sink fractions (similar approach in eq (5) of Röckmann et al., 2011). We also consider the atmospheric total $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and stratospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ lifetime to be 8.8 [8.3–9.4] years (our posterior mean for 2003–2012) and $1 5 2 \pm 2 4$ years (as adopted in Rigby et al. (2017)), respectively. Based on these assumptions, we derive the average sink fractions (and corresponding average atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ lifetimes) as follows: $89 \pm 2 \%$ (10.0 years) for tropospheric OH, $2 . 2 \pm 2 . 9 \%$ (409 years) for soil oxidation, and $3 . 2 \pm 1 . 1 \%$ (275 years) for tropospheric Cl. These estimates are generally consistent with bottom-up estimates in the Global Carbon Project (GCP) (Saunois et al., 2020). The poorly quantified sink contribution of tropospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } { - } \mathrm { C l }$ reactions is an important contributor to the uncertainty of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget estimated from $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ due to its large KIEC. Our estimated Cl contribution is lower than Allan et al. (2007), but higher than Gromov et al. (2018) where the tropospheric Cl contribution is almost zero. However, our derived sink-weighted KIEs are also sensitive to the selected KIEs in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ -OH reactions from the literature (Table S4). Further validation of Cl sink contributions and experimental studies on the KIEs are needed.
Comparison with Basu et al. (2022)

Basu et al. (2022) concluded from their sensitivity tests in the joint $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ inversion that the uncertainty in our knowledge of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ source signatures is almost never a leading driver of uncertainty in sectorial source partitioning and larger uncertainties are related to tropospheric Cl and OH fractionation. However, their sensitivity test only evaluated the former impact by replacing prior $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ signature maps for selected three sources (biomass burning, ruminants, oil/natural gas, and wetlands), respectively, and they did not evaluate the whole combined uncertainty related to all $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ - $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ source signatures. It is also noted such $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ signature maps are generally produced by extrapolating and smoothing the limited direct measurements, whose potential uncertainty is large, particularly in the region where the data number is limited (e.g., tropics). Under the situation, we believe it is possible the uncertainty of $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ source signatures they have explored is still underestimated and more careful treatment is required for evaluating their impact comprehensively. Another reason of the contradiction between Basu et al. (2022) and ours could be due to different consideration of uncertainty for BIO $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ signatures. While our one-box model approach can only treat the global average explicitly, they evaluated the uncertainty of prior emission maps (i.e. wetland inundation extent) and source signature maps, separately. Therefore, if they combined all the uncertainties related to biogenic sources, the impact of uncertainty in their BIO isotopic source signature would be larger than they reported. Although our simple sensitivity tests suggest the impact of whole uncertainty of BIO $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C - C H } _ { 4 }$ source signatures could be comparable to or even exceed that of total $\mathrm { K I E ^ { C } }$ when estimating the global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget (Fig. 11), we acknowledge further investigation using a 3D model is more reliable, which can resolve their spatial information.
